name: Women's rights
scope: Women's rights as the rights and entitlements claimed for women and girls: equal standing before the law and in the family, the vote and public office, property and contract, education, paid work and equal pay, bodily integrity, reproductive choice and freedom from violence. The defining sources are the women's rights movement as its own historians describe it (Schirmacher 1912, Ostrogorski 1893, from Wollstonecraft's 1792 Vindication and the 1848 Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments onward) and the UN's CEDAW and its Commission on the Status of Women (OHCHR/UN text). It covers the demand for equal rights as such, in any country or period. It excludes the wider body of feminist theory and its separate strands (radical, socialist, Islamic and other feminisms, which have their own entries) and positions of organisations beyond these rights claims.

summary: Women's rights is the claim that women and girls should hold the same legal, political, economic and civil rights as men. It runs from Wollstonecraft's Vindication and the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments through the suffrage movement to the 1979 UN CEDAW, covering the vote and public office, property and contract, education, work and equal pay, equal rights in marriage, divorce and parenthood, and access to family-planning information.
